title: Wele
author: Ghanaian tradition
desc: Singed, scraped, boiled six hours or more until moderately tender, then soaked overnight to leach the bitterness — a documented process with real safety caveats.
longDesc: Wele is singed cow hide and it is what gives the waakye tray its chew. It is published here as a documented process rather than a recipe, because no acceptable source publishes household quantities. The hide is cut into portions, rolled hair side out, tied, singed over a fire, washed thoroughly with a sponge and water, boiled six hours or more until moderately tender, soaked in water overnight to leach the bitter taste, and rinsed. The commercial practice carries real hazards that the research itself flags: scrap tyres as fuel, polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons, high microbial contamination and coliforms.
ingredients: Cow hide, cut into portions about 30 cm in length — see the note on the printed figure
Scrap wire or string, for tying
Water, for washing, boiling and the overnight soak
// No household quantities are published in any acceptable source. See the note.
equipment: A clean fire or gas burner, for singeing — NOT scrap tyres
Large bowl, for the overnight soak
steps: Cut the cow hide into portions and roll each one hair side out.
Tie the rolled ends with wire or string.
Singe over a fire until the hair is burnt off.
// SAFETY: use clean wood, charcoal or a gas burner. The documented commercial practice uses scrap tyres, which the research links to polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon contamination.
Scrape, then wash thoroughly with a sponge and water.
Boil in water in a large pot about six hours or more, until the hide becomes moderately tender.
Soak in water overnight, to leach out the bitter taste.
Add to soups, or to the waakye tray (GHA058).
chefTips: Moderately tender is the cue after six hours or more of boiling. Not soft — wele is meant to have real chew.
The overnight soak is not optional. It leaches a bitter taste that the singeing leaves behind, and skipping it is the usual reason home-prepared wele tastes wrong.
Singe over clean wood, charcoal or gas. The documented commercial practice in Accra uses scrap tyres as a cheap fuel, and the research flags polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon exposure as a consequence.

Wash thoroughly with a sponge after singeing. The research also reports high microbial contamination and the presence of coliforms in commercially prepared hide, so the washing and the long boil are both hygiene steps.
Rolled hair side out and tied before singeing. That is how the hide holds its shape over the flame.
Six hours is a long boil and it cannot be shortened. Collagen takes that long to give.
Published as a process. No named source gives household quantities and none have been invented.
commonMistakes: Singeing over scrap tyres or any burning plastic.
Skipping the overnight soak, which leaves it bitter.
Cutting the boil short, so it stays rubbery.
Boiling it to softness, which loses the texture entirely.
sources: PUBLISHED AS A DOCUMENTED PROCESS, NOT A HOUSEHOLD RECIPE. NO HOME-KITCHEN RECIPE EXISTS IN ANY ACCEPTABLE SOURCE, so there is no household-quantity entry and none has been invented. The ingredient list carries a header saying so.

PRIMARY SOURCE: Tettey E.C.-T., Osei-Yaw A., Hodari-Okae M., 'The quality of traditionally cooked cow hide as a source of food in Ghana', Ghana Journal of Agricultural Science 46. The authors' names print in OCR as 'E.C-T. TEITEY, A.OSEI-YAW & M.HODARE-OKAE'. Quantities and steps confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS). THE YEAR IS UNVERIFIED: one fetch gave 2013 and the other printed '(2008)'. Both are recorded.

PROCESS, steps as printed: 'The cow hide is first cut into portions about 30mm in length ... rolled (hair side out). The rolled ends are tied up with scrap wire.' Singed over 'a fire made below this arrangement from scrap tyres'. Then 'thoroughly wash with sponge and water.' Then 'boiled in water in large aluminium pots for about six hours or more until the hide becomes moderately tender'. Then 'soaked in water overnight' — one fetch adds: to leach the bitter taste. Then 'rinsed in clean water.'
DONENESS CUE, verbatim: 'until the hide becomes moderately tender'.

PROBABLE MISPRINT, flagged and NOT corrected: '30mm' for a rolled hide portion. Thirty millimetres is about an inch, which is implausibly small for something to be rolled and tied; thirty centimetres is the likely intention. The ingredient list above prints 30 cm with a pointer to this note, and the printed figure is given here so the reader can judge.

SAFETY WARNINGS PRINTED IN THE SOURCE'S OWN ABSTRACT, and reproduced because they matter: scrap-tyre singeing and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbon exposure; 'high contamination with micro-organisms'; and the presence of coliforms. These are the researchers' findings about commercially prepared wele, not editorial additions.
ALSO REPORTED: moisture content of cooked hide 'from 65.04 to 78.97 %'; sensory acceptability '3.12±0.32, (62.4%)'.

A SECOND SOURCE ON THE FUEL: Tettey E.C.T., 'Survey of processing of cattle hides into "wele" for sale as food in Ghana', 1988, an Accra survey. Its abstract states that 'scrap rubber tyres were used as a cheap source of fuel'. So the practice is documented across two studies two decades apart.

THE OLDEST RECORD, from Whitby 1968, a CSIR Food Research Institute bulletin: 'Cowhide, after scraping and soaking is cooked in soup as we/e.' — the OCR renders 'wele' as 'we/e'. Note that even in 1968 the scraping and soaking were the documented steps.

WHY THIS IS PUBLISHED DESPITE HAVING NO QUANTITIES: wele is a standard component of the waakye tray (GHA058) and appears in soups across southern Ghana, so a reader will meet it. Publishing the documented process WITH its safety findings stated is more useful than omitting it, since the hazards attach to how it is commercially prepared rather than to the food itself.
storage: 4 days refrigerated once cooked, or frozen.
healthBenefits: Almost pure collagen, so very high in glycine and proline.
High in protein and essentially free of carbohydrate.
Lower in fat than most offal.
The overnight soak and long boil both reduce surface contamination.
culturalNote: Wele is cheap protein that would otherwise be waste, and it is prized for texture rather than flavour — the chew is the point. That the published research on it is mostly about contamination from scrap-tyre fires says something uncomfortable about how the cheapest foods get made, and it is worth knowing before buying it ready-prepared.
